steps.body: Recursive rules read the same whatever the hop is. aₙ = aₙ₋₁ − 4 says “previous term minus 4”; aₙ = 3·aₙ₋₁ says “triple the previous term.” The symbol aₙ₋₁ always means one thing: **the term right before the one you're building.**
Work the chain, then jump past it.

widget.prompt: A sequence starts at 3. Set the step so that the 6th term is 23.
widget.successFeedback: d = 4: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23. Walking the chain works, but notice the formula does it in one hop — the 6th term is the start plus FIVE steps, not six. aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d, and that (n − 1) is where nearly every error lives.
widget.lowFeedback: The 6th term falls short of 23 — the step is too small.
widget.highFeedback: The 6th term overshoots 23 — the step is too big.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents sr recursive.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for sr recursive must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines sr recursive.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

predict.prompt: A sequence starts at 3 and its 6th term must be 23. The step you need is…
predict.reveal: 4. Getting from the 1st term to the 6th is FIVE hops, not six: 3 + 5×4 = 23. Counting the terms instead of the gaps between them is the most reliable way to land one step out, and it is why the formula carries (n − 1) rather than n.

explanationVariants: a₄ = 3·a₃ = 3·9 = 27 — the chain feeds each answer back in.

widget.prompt: Using a₁ = 1, aₙ = 3·aₙ₋₁, what is a₄?

commonErrors.feedback: 81 is a₅ — four triplings. The fourth term takes three: 1 → 3 → 9 → 27.
9 is a₃ — two triplings in. One more: 3 · 9 = 27.

steps.body: Here's recursion's superpower: the hop can be **anything**, even rules no single formula from Algebra 1 covers. a₁ = 1, aₙ = 2·aₙ₋₁ + 1 (“double, then add one”) builds 1, 3, 7, 15, … — not arithmetic, not geometric, yet the chain handles it effortlessly.

widget.prompt: Using a₁ = 1, aₙ = 2·aₙ₋₁ + 1, what is a₃?

commonErrors.feedback: 15 is a₄ — one hop too many. Two hops reach the third term: 1 → 3 → 7.
6 is 2·3 with the +1 dropped — the rule is double AND add one: 2·3 + 1 = 7.

explanationVariants: The rule computes a₅₀ from a₄₉, which needs a₄₈, and so on — the whole chain back to the start.
aₙ₋₁ isn't a formula in n: to use it you must actually hold the previous term.

widget.prompt: You want a₅₀ from a₁ = 7, aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 3 using ONLY the recursive rule. What does that require?

options.label: computing every term a₂ through a₄₉ first
options.feedback: Exactly — forty-eight hops before the one you wanted. That grind is recursion's one weakness.

options.label: substituting n = 50 directly
options.feedback: The rule's right side is a₄₉, not an expression in n — there's nothing for 50 to plug into until the previous term exists.

options.label: knowing the sequence's last term
options.feedback: Sequences build forward and this one never ends — there's no last term, and the rule only ever asks for the PREVIOUS one.

options.label: one multiplication: 50 · 3
options.feedback: 50·3 ignores the start and overcounts the hops. The one-line shortcut is 7 + 49·3 — and that's the EXPLICIT rule, not this one.

steps.body: So match the form to the job. “Next term?” — recursive, instantly. “Term number 100?” — explicit, one line. Recursive rules also shine when each value genuinely grows out of the last: balances updated month by month, populations updated season by season.
Match the tool to the question.

widget.prompt: Which rule form answers each question fastest?

items.label: What's the NEXT term after the one on my screen?
items.feedback: The next term is one hop from what you already have — that's the recursive rule's exact move; the explicit form would recompute from scratch.

items.label: What is a₁₀₀?
items.feedback: Jumping to a distant position is the explicit rule's one-line specialty — the recursive route would need ninety-nine hops.

items.label: Each month's balance is last month's plus $40 — track it month to month.
items.feedback: “Last month's plus $40” IS a next-from-previous instruction — the situation is already speaking recursively.

items.label: Jump straight to the value in row 25.
items.feedback: “Straight to row 25” means position → term with no chain — the explicit rule's job description.

widget.missFeedback: Match each question to the form that answers it without extra work: chains for next-step questions, one-line jumps for distant positions.
widget.successFeedback: Right tool, right question — that instinct is the whole point of having two forms.

explanationVariants: Three hops of “triple, subtract 1” starting from 2 land on 41.

widget.prompt: Using a₁ = 2, aₙ = 3·aₙ₋₁ − 1, what is a₄?

commonErrors.feedback: 14 is a₃ — one hop short. Feed it back in: 3·14 − 1 = 41.
122 is a₅ — you applied the rule to 41 itself. The fourth term IS 41; stop one hop sooner.

hints: Every hop is “triple the previous term, then subtract 1.”
a₂ = 3·2 − 1 = 5 — keep feeding each answer back into the rule.

steps.body: Chains handle any hop — at a price.
takeaways: aₙ₋₁ always means the term right before the one you're building.
Recursion covers rules no single nth-term formula does — like “double, add one.”
Its cost: distant terms need the whole chain. The explicit form is the cure.
steps.teaser: Next: converting between the two forms — so you always hold the right tool.

concept.body: Feed each answer back in — that's all a chain is. For a₁ = 5, aₙ = 2·aₙ₋₁: a₂ = 2·5 = 10, then a₃ = 2·10 = 20. The output of one hop is the input of the next.

widget.prompt: Using a₁ = 5, aₙ = 2·aₙ₋₁, what is a₃?

commonErrors.feedback: 40 is a₄ — three doublings. The third term takes two: 5 → 10 → 20.
10 is a₂ — halfway there. Double once more: 2·10 = 20.
